Three LevelBlue security experts put their investigative skills to the test in the SentinelOne Threat Hunting competition, with Jodie McDonald earning the top spot in EMEA and advancing to the Grand Final at OneCon.

Threat hunting requires more than knowing your way around a security platform. It takes curiosity, analytical thinking, and the discipline to follow the evidence, even when it leads somewhere unexpected.

Three LevelBlue security experts recently demonstrated those skills on a global stage, earning standout results in the SentinelOne Threat Hunting competition. Jodie McDonald, Senior DFIR Consultant, finished No. 1 in EMEA, securing her place in the Grand Final against the top competitors from the Americas and Asia. Rishi Aggarwal, Senior Security Solutions Architect, ranked in the top 15 in the Asia Regional Final, while Eni Zeqo, Senior DFIR Consultant, placed among the top 25 competitors in EMEA.

The competition challenged participants to investigate alerts, logs, and evidence across four areas: Endpoint, Cloud, Data & AI, and Securing AI. Working against the clock, competitors had to uncover the story behind the data, distinguish meaningful signals from noise, and deliver accurate answers under pressure.

For the LevelBlue team, the experience was an opportunity to test their skills, explore evolving security technologies, and put their real-world investigative experience to work in unfamiliar scenarios.

Following the evidence, not just the alerts

For digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) professionals, an alert is only the beginning of an investigation. Understanding what happened, how it happened, and what else might be affected requires looking beyond the initial signal.

That mindset was central to how all three competitors approached the challenge.

“When faced with large volumes of alerts, I would typically first try and categorize by alert type to determine the most high fidelity alerts,” McDonald explained. “Then, further down the line with the context I have gained from the higher fidelity alerts, I would look at the alerts such as lateral movement, and do queries around that to gain full understanding of threat actor activities.”

Zeqo emphasized the importance of prioritization, particularly when investigating a potentially active incident.

“It is important, just as it was in the competition, that we provide precise answers within the shortest window of time possible to reduce the risk of the incident spreading further if we are dealing with a live threat.”

For Aggarwal, building a reliable timeline is essential to separating meaningful evidence from an isolated alert.

“I normally start with the things I can trust, such as timestamps, identities, devices, process activity and network connections. I build a quick timeline and look for one or two strong anchors,” he said. “The trail worth following is usually the one that explains several pieces of evidence, rather than simply the alert that looks the most serious at first.”

Although their professional backgrounds differ, the three approaches share a common principle: effective threat hunting means connecting the dots rather than stopping at the first plausible explanation.

Stop hidden threats before damage is done.

Learn More

Curiosity is what separates a good threat hunter from a great one

Technical expertise provides the foundation for threat hunting, but the ability to question assumptions and investigate beyond the obvious is what turns individual findings into a fuller understanding of an incident.

“I would say being curious,” McDonald said when asked what separates an excellent threat hunter from someone who simply knows the technology. “Seeing an alert and knowing what it means is good, and gives a finding, but the natural curiosity to want to dig deeper makes for a richer finding.”

That curiosity can mean investigating how a suspicious executable arrived on a system, what happened before and after an alert, or whether the same activity appears elsewhere in an environment.

Aggarwal described the same instinct as a combination of curiosity and discipline.

“Curiosity, discipline and a willingness to be wrong. Knowing the technology is important, but a good threat hunter also questions their first assumption, follows the evidence and can explain why a conclusion makes sense.”

It is a particularly important skill in a competition environment, where participants have limited time to investigate each scenario. This year's challenge gave competitors just 30 minutes to answer eight questions in a round.

McDonald and Zeqo both found that knowing when to move on was just as important as knowing when to dig deeper. If an answer did not emerge after a few minutes, they would switch to another question and return later if time allowed.

For Aggarwal, the decision came down to whether an investigative path was producing useful evidence.

“If a few pivots did not produce anything useful, I parked that hypothesis and tested another one,” he explained. “That did not mean the original idea was necessarily wrong. It just meant it was not producing enough evidence to justify spending more time on it at that point.”

That balance between persistence and adaptability is essential in a timed challenge and in real-world investigations where thoroughness and speed can both have significant consequences.

Putting security technology to the test

The competition also gave participants an opportunity to explore SentinelOne capabilities beyond their usual workflows, including Purple AI, which can help analysts formulate queries and identify investigative leads.

McDonald and Zeqo both use Purple AI to develop queries that support threat hunting, while emphasizing the importance of validating results and understanding the underlying data.

“Whilst Purple AI then returns the results, for myself I typically will then go and run that query myself, as I am mindful that sometimes AI can be wrong, and it’s important in an investigation to know that the data returned is completely accurate,” McDonald said.

Aggarwal took a similar approach, using AI to accelerate his initial investigation without handing over the responsibility for the final conclusion.

“I used Purple AI to help me get oriented, phrase questions and identify possible pivots more quickly. I treated its responses as leads rather than final answers. Any conclusion still had to match the underlying telemetry and timeline.”

The competition also pushed the participants into less familiar territory. McDonald and Aggarwal identified Securing AI as their biggest stretch, while Zeqo found Cloud more challenging because she had fewer opportunities to explore that area in her day-to-day work.

Those unfamiliar scenarios made the experience particularly valuable. As McDonald put it, the competition offers a chance to test emerging features before encountering them in a real client investigation.

“I think just how fun it is and how much you can learn! SentinelOne, and other platforms for threat hunting competitions, are always adding new features that we may not have an opportunity to experience in the wild.”

For security professionals, that combination of practical experience and experimentation helps build familiarity with new capabilities before they may be needed in a live investigation.

Three standout achievements

Each LevelBlue competitor brought a different set of experiences to the challenge and each came away with a result worth celebrating.

Jodie McDonald: No. 1 in EMEA

McDonald’s path to the top spot came with an unexpected twist. She initially believed she had finished third in the EMEA Regional Final. Later that evening, emails from SentinelOne suggested otherwise. The following morning, she learned that two competitors ranked above her had been disqualified for cheating, confirming her first-place finish.

“At first I couldn’t believe it, since I thought I had come third, so it did take me a little bit to process that actually I had won it!”

Now, McDonald is preparing to represent EMEA in the Grand Final at OneCon, where she will compete against the top-ranked hunters from the Americas and Asia.

Her strategy is to rely on the same methodical approach that brought her through the earlier rounds and not let the clock dictate her investigation.

“As hard as it is, I try to pretend like the clock isn’t there, and try to treat it like I am doing an actual DFIR investigation.”

Rather than focusing solely on the question in front of her, she aims to follow natural investigative paths, collect useful context, and recognize that an answer to one question may emerge while investigating another.

Rishi Aggarwal: A top-15 Asia Regional Finalist

Aggarwal ranked among the top 15 competitors in Asia and highlighted his ability to adapt across all four competition areas. With only a few months of SentinelOne experience, he also finished first in three qualifier games, earned three trophies, and ranked first in the combined Asia qualifier standings, according to his competition results.

“I’m most proud of adapting quickly and staying competitive across four very different areas,” he said. “The experience also gave me a much better understanding of how my existing SIEM and investigation skills could transfer into SentinelOne.”

Aggarwal also acknowledged Grant Hutchons, LevelBlue Director of Security Solutions Engineering for APAC, for introducing him to SentinelOne and encouraging him to participate, as well as the support he received from Grant and LevelBlue throughout the experience.

Eni Zeqo: A top-25 EMEA competitor

Zeqo finished among the top 25 competitors in EMEA, drawing on her DFIR experience and the knowledge she gained working closely with LevelBlue's Threat Monitoring and Containment (TMAC) team.

“I am proud to have been able to compete alongside peers in the industry with such vast knowledge and still place relatively high in the leaderboards,” she said.

She credits her experience working with the TMAC team for helping her learn how to navigate endpoint detection and response platforms, particularly SentinelOne, and apply those skills in the competition.

Her results reflect both the value of hands-on investigative experience and the importance of continually learning from colleagues and new challenges.

Together, these achievements demonstrate the depth of investigative talent across LevelBlue and the value of bringing different technical backgrounds and perspectives to complex security challenges.

Next stop: OneCon

With the Grand Final approaching, McDonald has one more challenge ahead: competing against the top threat hunters from across the Americas, EMEA, and Asia.

Her preparation comes down to staying calm, trusting her investigative instincts, and remembering that the answer is not always immediately apparent.

“There were many questions within the qualifiers and EMEA final where I found the answer later on whilst working on another question and not even looking for the answer to the original question,” she said. “I think just keeping in mind that I may find the answers whilst working on another question and to not stress!”

It is advice that applies well beyond a competition. Effective threat hunting depends on staying curious, questioning assumptions, and allowing the evidence to tell the story.

Congratulations to Jodie, Rishi, and Eni on their impressive performances. As Jodie heads to OneCon to compete for the global title, the LevelBlue team will be cheering her on. Good luck, Jodie!

articles.title: Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver: The Trust Gap Attackers Operate Inside
articles.context: Public threat research found a single GitHub PFX file holding more than a dozen expired certificates, drawn from the 2015 Hacking Team leak and Chinese forums
articles.full_text:
Bring your own vulnerable driver (BYOVD) is having a moment in endpoint security. Some of the buzz is earned. Some of it is overblown. This series unpacks both and shows the evidence for each. This piece weighs the trust gap the technique exploits against what the data actually shows.

A long-revoked certificate still loads a driver into the Windows kernel today. Help Net Security traced a 2026 intrusion to a decade-old forensic driver whose signing certificate had expired and been revoked years earlier. The kernel loaded it anyway.

The reason is structural, and it explains why the defensive target most teams chase is the wrong one. Defenders track bad drivers. We pull the LOLDrivers catalog, sync the default driver blocklist, and watch the list grow. The list is not where attackers compete. They compete over signing trust. A signature is the scarce thing. A driver is just the disposable wrapper around it.

Trust Is the Scarce Resource and Drivers are Disposable

Think about a stolen credit card. The number keeps clearing for hours or days in the gap before merchant blocklists sync. The thief does not need a new card. They need the window where the old one still works. Card networks did not win by perfecting the blocklist. They won by scoring the transaction itself in real time, regardless of whether the number was flagged yet.

Signed drivers run on the same broken model. The blocklist is the merchant blocklist. The signature is the card. Attackers live in the propagation gap, and that gap is wide.

The defensive move that follows is to stop chasing the card numbers and instrument the transaction. This is the reframe no competitor owns. Defend the trust anchor, because the list will always trail it. The anchor is the signing trust itself: revocation, signature metadata, and the slow death of cross-signed-driver trust. A list of bad drivers grows forever. The set of trust mechanisms that let those drivers load is small and addressable.

The web learned this lesson the hard way already. Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) soft-fail meant a browser that could not reach the revocation responder simply trusted the certificate anyway. The kernel driver model carries the same flaw in a harsher setting. There is no soft-fail to debate, because the kernel does not ask the question at all.

The Proof Is In the Certificates

The economics favor the attacker because trust concentrates. Public threat research found a single GitHub PFX file holding more than a dozen expired certificates, drawn from the 2015 Hacking Team leak and Chinese forums. That one file forged signatures on thousands of malicious drivers.

A small set of compromised keys signs an unbounded supply of drivers. A few stolen keys against thousands of drivers means the list defenders maintain can never catch up. Block a driver and the cost is one recompile. Edit unauthenticated bytes, the file hash changes, and the same key signs a new artifact. The blocklist entry you just earned is already stale, because the signing key did not move and the key is the asset. SentinelOne®'s latest Annual Threat Report documents loaders that reintroduce effectively the same payload under fresh hashes to outpace simple hash-based blocking.

The trust-pyramid framing from that research describes a real structure. At the base sit individual drivers, cheap and disposable. Above them sit the end-entity certificates that sign batches of drivers, and at the apex sit the cross-signed certificate authorities the kernel anchors to. An attacker who climbs one level multiplies their reach across everything below it, and defenders who fight at the base are fighting where the attacker has infinite supply.

The same research showed how attackers manufacture fresh trust on demand. Tools forge signature timestamps, exploiting the pre-July-29-2015 cross-signed certificate exception by backdating a signature so it appears to predate the cutoff. An expired or revoked certificate becomes a working signing key again. The forgery does not break the trust chain. It satisfies it.

The kernel makes this worse by refusing to check revocation. Windows loads drivers signed with revoked certificates even when a local revocation list is present, and the decade-old forensic driver case showed the same failure in 2026. The operating system's kernel-mode signing policy accepts end-entity certificates issued before July 29, 2015 if they chain to a cross-signed authority. The policy codifies the loophole rather than closing it.

The defensive consequence follows directly. Blocking expired and revoked certificate driver loads, paired with the blocklist, beats the blocklist alone. The blocklist enumerates known-bad files one at a time. Revocation enforcement attacks the reusable key behind all of them, scaling against the attacker instead of with them.

A certificate authority revokes a key when it learns the key is compromised, and in a working system every consumer checks the revocation list and refuses the key. A revoked certificate carries a clear instruction, do not trust anything this key signs, and the kernel loads the driver anyway. The attacker did not defeat the trust system. They used the part of it that was never enforced.

The Driver Persistence Half-Life

Now the data. Against the LOLDrivers catalog, roughly one-third of catalogued vulnerable driver samples are not covered by the default blocklist. The June 19, 2026 pull puts it at 36 percent. That is 782 of 2,190 samples, absent from the default list. About 22 percent, 479 samples, load even with Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity (HVCI) enabled.

Call this the Driver Persistence Half-Life, the signature data point of this argument.

Be honest about what that number is. The 36 and 22 percent figures are point estimates from a single computed pull against one blocklist version. The method is published and reproducible: parse the enforced HVCI SiPolicy and the official block rules against the LOLDrivers JSON, match by file hash, then by authenticode metadata, and pin both to a commit and a version.

The caveats matter. The denominator is the LOLDrivers catalog, not every driver that exists. "Not covered" means absent from the default block rules, not exploitable on a given host. Hash coverage is brittle, because an edit to unauthenticated bytes changes the hash without changing the abuse.

The corroboration is real, and it is fewer voices than it looks. The catalog's own coverage metrics report that many LOLDrivers entries sit off the default blocklist, and public threat research corroborates the cadence qualitatively, confirming that systems can be attacked with a driver not yet listed. Two open tools reproduce the check itself, Trail of Bits' HVCI-loldrivers-check and a community block-rules checker, but no genuinely independent second count of the exact figures exists yet.

The lag underneath the number is the real exposure. The default blocklist updates only periodically through Windows Update, roughly once or twice a year, and deliberately holds back some blocks to avoid breaking legitimate software. The minimum disclosure-to-block window is a calendar quarter, and the historical window has run to six months or more. Most of these vulnerable signed drivers are reachable without admin rights, so the exposure is wide and the door is low.

The on-device reality runs worse than the stated cadence. Public reporting documented a Windows 10 driver blocklist frozen at a December 2019 version until an October 2022 fix. That is a roughly three-year gap between the published cadence and what shipped on the machine. A defender reading the cadence would assume quarterly freshness. The endpoint disagreed for three years.

Per case, persistence runs to years. SentinelLABS disclosed Dell's dbutil_2_3.sys flaws in 2021, and the signed-but-vulnerable driver was still disabling security tooling in 2024. SentinelLABS noted that the driver's certificate had not been revoked, leaving it abusable long after disclosure.

The half-life metaphor is precise. The catalog grows faster than the blocklist can absorb it, so the gap widens rather than closes, a long, slow decay that the attacker schedules around.

The method is reproducible against your own fleet. Run the same hash and authenticode match against the drivers that actually load, and the result is a number that describes your real exposure, a measurement you can repeat each quarter. The durable claim stays the honest one: roughly one-third of catalogued vulnerable drivers are not blocked by default. The precise 36 and 22 percent belong to one computed pull, a snapshot with a published method attached.

Blocking Everything Breaks the Business

The obvious fix is to block every old driver. That fix is impractical, and the platform's own documentation says so plainly: the blocklist "isn't guaranteed to block every driver," and blocks are held back precisely to avoid breaking functionality.

Vulnerable drivers are dual-use. Public threat research catalogued how most abused drivers ship as legitimate software components first. The same signed driver that disables an EDR this week was a working hardware utility last week. The blocklist maintainer weighs one confirmed abuse against tens of thousands of working installs. The hold-back is a rational choice under that math, and the exact gap the attacker schedules into.

The reboot gap makes the DIY approach worse. Independent analysis of the blocklist notes that a driver the policy would block keeps running until the next reboot, so an in-progress kill chain survives the moment you activate the policy. The attack surface reduction (ASR) rule that blocks vulnerable signed drivers only stops a driver from being written to disk. It does not block one already present from loading. Defenders who think they have closed the gap have often only narrowed the entry path.

The platform is moving the trust anchor. A Windows security update in April 2026 removes default trust for cross-signed kernel drivers, directly targeting the loophole the timestamp-forgery and pre-2015 exceptions opened. This is the industry bending toward the right target, attacking the reusable signing key itself, which is the correct altitude.

It helps. It does not close the gap. The April change applies to default trust going forward, so the 36 percent that sit off the blocklist today are not retroactively addressed by changing tomorrow's trust rules. The half-life keeps running on the inventory that already exists.

A separate chokepoint also remains in play. Public threat research documented one EDR killer used by multiple ransomware gangs whose coordination point was a shared packer-as-a-service, with no shared driver tying them together. The packer became the chokepoint when the driver did not. That is the pattern to internalize. Each fix narrows one path and exposes the next. Tighten cross-signed trust and the attacker leans harder on forged timestamps. Close the timestamp loophole and they lean on the unsynced backlog. The trust model has many anchors, and the attacker only needs the cheapest one still standing.

This persistence is not an accident of the technique. It is the product of an industry on the other side. SentinelOne's latest Annual Threat Report describes the industrialization of the modern cyber breach, with mature automation accelerating intrusions at scale. A trust gap that one researcher could exploit becomes one that a tooled-up criminal market exploits at volume, which is why the half-life persists across so many drivers at once.

This piece builds on prior work. Independent security research argued that admin-to-kernel is not a serviced security boundary and that blocklists are largely performative. That critique is correct and it stands. The contribution here is a measured persistence half-life, the certificate-concentration evidence behind it, and a trust-anchor reframe detection engineers can act on.

Stop Chasing the List. Instrument the Failure.

The card networks made the stolen number unprofitable by scoring the transaction. Defenders should do the same with signed drivers. Watch the trust event, because the catalog entry arrives too late to matter.

That means instrumenting the load itself. Sysmon Event ID 6 logs every driver load with its hash, signer, signature, and signature status, and any non-Valid status warrants investigation. This telemetry is low-volume and high-value, which makes it cheap to monitor and hard to flood. The Splunk detection content keys on exactly this event, with an explicit note that the alert needs triage rather than blind firing.

Signature-status detection and first-seen anomaly detection catch what blocklist matching misses. Alert on any driver load whose signature status is not Valid, including untrusted root, explicit distrust, and bad or invalid signatures, and on any driver whose hash, signer, or version has never been seen on the host before. Both approaches key on the trust attribute, so the known-bad list never enters the decision and the alert fires whether or not anyone has catalogued the driver yet.

The CodeIntegrity Operational log confirms whether your blocklist policy actually applied. Event ID 3099 confirms the policy is loaded, a blocked load logs Event ID 3077, an audited load logs Event ID 3076, and Event ID 3089 carries the signature detail. Pairing the block events with the audit events proves which drivers the policy stopped, which turns coverage from an assumption into a measurement. Given the three-year staleness the frozen-blocklist case showed, that proof is not optional.

The behavioral chain is observable end to end. A service is created via sc.exe, logged as Sysmon Event ID 1, and a System Event 7045 fires for the service install. A driver loads under Event ID 6, then a device control call (IOCTL) drives termination against protected processes. Public threat research watched one such loop run a repeating, fixed-interval termination cycle in kernel mode, stepping past protected-process defenses (PPL), and recent killers also unregister EDR kernel callbacks as a distinct observable before terminating processes. Picus mapped the same sequence across cases. Each step is a tripwire on the trust event, and none of it depends on prior knowledge of the specific driver.

The order of the chain is what makes it durable. The driver name changes every campaign, but the structure does not. SentinelOne's latest Annual Threat Report makes the same point about the kernel: activity at that layer can blind user-space instrumentation and leave a manual disk scan an unreliable assurance of cleanliness. Detection keyed to that shape survives a recompile, and detection keyed to a hash does not.

The mental shift is the point. A driver list is a finite answer to an infinite problem, and the trust anchor is small, addressable, and already moving. SentinelLABS research has lived at that anchor for years. The team co-discovered the POORTRY and STONESTOP WHQL-signed toolkit that drove the security advisory ADV220005, and proposed Authenticode-metadata blocklisting before that was standard practice.

Defenders are not behind because the list is incomplete. They are behind because they were grading the wrong exam. Score the trust event, and the half-life stops being the attacker's advantage.

Why This Is the Work SentinelOne Exists To Do

Scoring the trust event instead of chasing the list is the whole argument, and it is the argument SentinelOne was built to win. The platform watches the load itself, the untrusted signature, the first-seen driver, and the masquerading kernel service, from a vantage designed to keep reporting when the kernel turns hostile. Purple AI® carries that telemetry forward. Its Agentic Investigation capability reasons over the trust event the moment it fires, builds the timeline, and renders a verdict in minutes and seconds rather than hours and days. The propagation gap the attacker lives inside narrows when the verdict arrives at machine speed.

A control you have not confirmed is running is a control you are only hoping for, and most teams cannot staff that verification around the clock. Wayfinder, SentinelOne's managed detection and response practice, holds the line when your own team is asleep, fusing human threat hunting with the platform's autonomous investigation and Google threat intelligence. That is the reason the company exists. The trust anchor is small and addressable, and the advantage goes to the defender who instruments it.

Next in this series: The practical hunts themselves, the four distinct techniques hiding inside the phrase EDR killer, and the telemetry that catches each one.

Bring your own vulnerable driver (BYOVD) is having a moment in endpoint security. Some of the buzz is earned. Some of it is overblown. This series unpacks both and shows the evidence for each. This piece traces how the technique scaled into an industry.

Ransomware actors successfully disabled security tools in about 48% of intrusions in 2024. That figure comes from security researchers, drawn from incident-response engagements across the year. Attackers attempted to blind the defender in most of those cases. They almost always succeeded. Turning off the sensor was once a flourish. It is now a default move.

That 48% is the broad rate for disabling security tools by any method. BYOVD is the kernel-level technique this series tracks, one fast-growing method inside that number, and public threat research treats it as the part of the tamper problem accelerating fastest. Treat the 48% as the ceiling and the BYOVD slice as the piece that scaled into a market.

The Claim: This Became a Supply Chain

EDR killing industrialized over the last several years. SentinelOne®'s latest Annual Threat Report, "Defending Against the Industrialization of the Modern Cyber Breach," names that shift directly, with mature automation accelerating intrusions and tradecraft moving from one-off effort to maintained capability. A killer was once a binary an intruder wrote and discarded. Today it is a serviced capability, built, versioned, and bundled into ransomware-as-a-service for affiliates who never touch a debugger. The defender once faced a hobbyist. Now the defender faces a development pipeline.

A pipeline behaves differently from a one-off binary. It ships versions, fixes bugs, and reuses code across releases. The defender reads that cadence like a vendor roadmap, and every release leaves the same observable footprint when it runs. The reuse is visible in the architecture. Public threat reporting describes one current framework spinning eight-plus variants off a single shared design. That also means a detection tuned to one variant often catches its siblings. Code reuse cuts both ways, and the defender holds one of the edges.

The Proof: A Four-Year Timeline

Start at the floor. Public threat research documented an early Process Explorer-driver killer in 2023, used to disable EDR ahead of Medusa Locker and LockBit. The same year, SentinelLABS tracked an actor called "Spyboy" selling the Terminator killer. The price ran from $300 for a single AV bypass to $3,000 for the all-in-one EDR killer, and the tool abused Zemana drivers. These were early-window artifacts. They were standalone, sold, and disposable.

That timeline has a SentinelLABS anchor that reframes the whole story. SentinelLABS attributed the AvNeutralizer killer, also known as AuKill, to the FIN7 cybercrime group. FIN7 sold it on Russian-language forums at prices running from $4,000 to $15,000. The tool abused a Time Travel Debugging driver and the Process Explorer driver to disable defenses. This is the moment a killer stopped being a one-off and became a product with a price list.

The adoption pattern proves the product framing. SentinelLABS tracked AvNeutralizer spreading into Black Basta, AvosLocker, MedusaLocker, BlackCat, Trigona, and LockBit operations. One group built it, and six competing crews ran it. A single tool crossing that many rivals is the signature of a supplier, and the new feature was distribution.

Then the model changed inside ransomware-as-a-service. In August 2024, public reporting disclosed EDRKillShifter, abusing the RentDrv2 and ThreatFireMonitor drivers and first seen in a RansomHub attack. Researchers assessed with moderate confidence that the tool served multiple attackers, not RansomHub alone. The SentinelOne RansomHub anthology records the affiliate logic behind that spread, a customized EDR-killer tool made available to higher-level affiliates. One crew's tool became many crews' tool, and the new feature was tiered access.

The driver roster widened fast across 2025. In early 2025, public threat research documented a malicious driver that carried stolen, revoked certificates and imitated a legitimate EDR driver to silence defenses inside Medusa intrusions. By August 2025, GuidePoint tracked Akira affiliates in SonicWall VPN intrusions chaining a ThrottleStop driver, rwdrv.sys, with a malicious helper, hlpdrv.sys, to disable the built-in Windows antivirus. Different crews, different drivers, the same kernel-level objective. SentinelOne's latest Annual Threat Report records the same pattern from the other side of the kill, naming crews that script the built-in Windows antivirus into silence and kernel-mode drivers derived from POORTRY used to terminate EDR processes and delete security files.

The CVE-anchored cases arrived next. In December 2025, security researchers documented DeadLock ransomware abusing the Baidu antivirus driver BdApiUtil, tracked as CVE-2024-51324, to terminate EDR and the built-in Windows antivirus. In February 2026, public reporting documented Reynolds ransomware embedding the vulnerable NSecsoft driver NSecKrnl, tracked as CVE-2025-68947, which terminated more than 30 security processes. Those CVE records do not name the ransomware, and the actor mapping comes from threat intel. The same NSecKrnl driver shows up across unrelated crews, tied to Reynolds and to Warlock. A driver is shared infrastructure, so pivoting on the driver hash groups campaigns by supplier, not by gang.

By 2025 the sharing went structural. Threat-intel reporting found one EDR killer used across several competing ransomware families, distributed as distinct per-attack packed builds, and Singapore's national cyber agency corroborated the same multi-group pattern in an August 2025 advisory, independent of any single vendor. Public threat research also catalogued a forming marketplace of named killers priced from hundreds to thousands of dollars. Rivals were now buying from a common counter.

The 2026 picture is operator-run kits with large affiliate cuts. Public threat reporting documented the Gentlemen RaaS shipping its in-house EDR killer framework, running eight-plus BYOVD variants and targeting over 400 processes across 48 security products through DeviceIoControl calls. The operator reportedly hands affiliates around a 90% revenue share, a 10% operator cut against a 20% industry standard, and bundles third-party killers like HexKiller and ThrottleBlood. By April 2026, researchers saw Qilin and Warlock at the same game, Qilin chaining the rwdrv.sys and hlpdrv.sys pair while Warlock ran NSecKrnl. Public threat research now reads EDR killers as a standard, repeatable phase of the attack playbook. SentinelOne's latest Annual Threat Report measured how far the response window has collapsed, with one chained sequence reaching SYSTEM in roughly 30 milliseconds and a separate intrusion moving from initial download to a persistent service in 49 seconds.

The Turn: Acceleration Over Origination

Here is the correction the timeline forces. Commercial sale of EDR killers predates the 2024 window. SentinelLABS had Terminator on the market in 2023 and dated FIN7's AvNeutralizer sales earlier still. ExtraHop tracked a dark-web market for these tools across 2024 and 2025. Older still, the open-source EDRSandblast project weaponized a vulnerable driver against more than 1,000 security drivers back in 2022. The raw capability was for sale before the surge.

So the real story is acceleration and consolidation. The non-obvious shift is that rival ransomware crews stopped competing on this layer and started sharing it instead. Several groups feeding from one killer is a market choosing a common supplier. The cost of building beats the cost of buying.

The economics pulled the skill floor down. Reynolds ransomware bundled a vulnerable driver as a recruiting selling point aimed at less-skilled operators, and a capability that once required a kernel developer now requires a subscription. The driver is the part most likely to fail in unskilled hands, so researchers documented a practice they call driver decoupling. Affiliates install the vulnerable driver and confirm it loads before running the killer. That is the kind of guardrail a supplier adds to keep low-skill customers successful, packaging doing the work the operator used to do by hand.

What Makes Consolidation Possible

Markets need shared infrastructure, and this one has it. The shared killer that reporting tracked was one tool reissued as distinct packed builds for each attack, with the packer as the common chokepoint several rivals fed through. Singapore's advisory described the same customized-build distribution model, a single supplier serving many buyers.

The driver supply explains why it scales. Public reference lists now track thousands of vulnerable signed drivers, most reachable without admin rights. The live LOLDrivers catalogue alone records hundreds of unique drivers, a large share still missing from the default driver blocklist. That inventory reads as a parts catalog for the kit builder, a dual-use commodity supply where weak driver access controls hand unprivileged users a way in.

The price ladder runs from the low hundreds for Terminator to five figures for FIN7's AvNeutralizer, both tracked by SentinelLABS, while EDRKillShifter spread through tiered affiliate access rather than a flat price. The skill floor drops in step. EDRSandblast showed the open-source baseline back in 2022, already capable against more than 1,000 security drivers, and a buyer in 2026 does not need that depth. The operator maintains the tool and the affiliate just runs it, so each layer of packaging removes a reason an attacker would have failed. A working tool spreads fast once the price of entry drops to a download.

The Payoff: A Top-Tier Threat Getting Cheaper

Put the pieces together and the threat ranking is clear. Disabling defense is attempted in most ransomware intrusions and succeeds in roughly half. The tooling that does it is now maintained, shared across rivals, and sold with affiliate economics that reward volume. Each force lowers cost and widens reach at once. This is a structural threat, and it is getting cheaper to run.

Defenders set the response, and the response is not despair. Public threat research shows BYOVD remains the dominant kill method, and that dominance means the kill chain stays observable. The killer still has to act in a fixed sequence. It installs a driver, registers a kernel service, and issues the calls that terminate the sensor. Those steps leave telemetry behind them.

The defender should still hold the technique apart from its cousins. BYOVD is one entry in a tamper taxonomy. A driverless class is smaller but growing, and it skips the driver-install step entirely. EDR-Freeze suspends the sensor through a Windows error-reporting race, staying fully in user mode. EDRSilencer uses Windows filtering rules to block the sensor's telemetry from leaving the host. Those two break the driver-load observable, so a detection built only around driver loads will miss them.

Prevention narrows the window without closing it, which is exactly why behavioral observables carry weight. The sequence is concrete enough to map to event IDs. Picus Security described the early steps of the BYOVD chain as logged events. A service created with sc.exe surfaces as a Sysmon process-create record (Event ID 1) and a System service-install event (Event ID 7045). The driver load surfaces as a Sysmon driver-load record (Event ID 6). The killer then issues its DeviceIoControl call, followed by callback removal and security-process termination. Each arrow in that chain is a place to correlate and alert.

The behavior inside that chain is even more specific. Public threat research documented a kill loop where a masquerading kernel service enumerates running processes on a repeating, fixed-interval cycle. It passes the process IDs through an IOCTL so the driver calls the kernel termination routine directly, bypassing the protected-process protections that guard the sensor. The repeating rekill cadence is itself a signal, because a normal service does not poll the process list and terminate from kernel mode on a loop.

Callback removal deserves its own hunt, separate from the kill. SOC Prime documented Qilin loading rwdrv.sys for raw memory read and write, then loading hlpdrv.sys to remove the EDR's registered kernel callbacks across more than 300 products. Stripping callbacks blinds the sensor without terminating its process. The process still runs and still reports healthy. The defender who only watches for a killed process misses this entirely.

The masquerade is its own tell. Frameworks ship variants that each impersonate a legitimate product to blend into a normal driver inventory, and one documented driver carried stolen, revoked certificates to imitate a real EDR driver. The defender's answer is to treat the signer and the first-seen status as data. Splunk detection content keys on any driver load whose signature status is not Valid. Alert on a driver whose hash, signer, or version has never appeared on the host before.

The witnesses also outlast the endpoint. Once the sensor is silenced, network, identity, and cloud telemetry are what remain, and independent analysis found EDR-killer execution preceding ransomware across multiple gangs, a window enough to intervene before encryption. Singapore's national cyber agency framed EDR-killer activity as huntable through driver-load monitoring, termination patterns, and telemetry cessation. An agent's health drop, a lost heartbeat, or a gap in a constant feed all read as tamper, so alert on the absence of expected signal. A high-fidelity variant is System Event ID 7031, the service-crash log Windows writes when a kill abruptly terminates a security service. It is rare in a healthy environment, which makes it a strong candidate for a tight, low-false-positive alert.

The mental shift for the practitioner is this. Stop modeling the EDR killer as an exotic, once-a-year event and start modeling it as supply.
